consensus_summary: The phrase identifies Jesus’ grave/tomb or, more broadly, the realm or state of the dead between his death and resurrection.
book_summary: The phrase identifies Jerusalem as the symbolic navel and heart of the land.
consensus_core_identification: Jesus’ place or state of burial/death.
book_core_identification: Jerusalem, understood as the central heart of the land.
boundary_disagreement: This is not merely a dispute over whether the referent includes both the tomb and Hades. The book replaces the death-and-burial referent with a geographical-symbolic identification of Jerusalem.
material_contradiction: In Matthew 12:40, the consensus takes Jesus’ being in the “heart of the earth” as his burial or presence among the dead; the book instead takes the location to be Jerusalem. These cannot serve as the same immediate identification in the same contextual sense without reclassifying the saying.
rationale: The book’s reading is divergent because it replaces the consensus’s central referent rather than narrowing or broadening it. It is not novel: the blind responses explicitly recognize Jerusalem or the heart of the land as a minority or rare alternative.
strongest_objection: Ezekiel 5:5 and 38:12 support describing Jerusalem as centrally situated among the nations or in the land, but they do not by themselves establish that Matthew 12:40 uses “heart of the earth” for Jerusalem. Matthew’s direct Jonah analogy more naturally supports confinement in death, the grave, or Hades.
